title: Respond humanely to a minor wrong without erasing a boundary

sections.title: Understand the distinction
sections.body: Compassion recognizes another person’s humanity; accountability identifies action and repair; forgiveness is a freely chosen relation to the wrong. None automatically restores access, trust or a loan privilege.

sections.title: Complete fictional practice material
sections.body: A book owner finds a torn removable cover after a loan. Borrower acknowledges the accidental tear and offers the agreed replacement cover costing 3 units. Owner wants the cover replaced and future lending paused. No other damage or malicious intention is supplied; private communication is welcome.

sections.title: Work through the supplied case
sections.body: Write a humane response preserving truth, the repair request and the lending limit. Distinguish these from humiliation or a demand for emotional reassurance.

sections.title: Try a different case before checking
sections.body: An owner refuses a new loan while speaking respectfully and seeking no revenge. Does that alone prove a failure to forgive?

checks.title: Compare reasoning and review the supplied result
checks.body: Accept or discuss the proportionate cover repair and state the future lending limit without an insult. Later fiction: the cover is replaced; the owner still declines another loan. Repair occurred, trust restoration is not established. Partial: be kind but omit the actual boundary. Incorrect: publish the borrower’s private details or demand an expensive unrelated gift.
criteria: Repair is proportionate to supplied harm
Boundaries do not require restored trust

checks.title: Check the changed case
checks.body: No. A lending boundary can remain even if forgiveness is freely chosen. The record cannot diagnose the owner’s internal state from the refusal alone.
criteria: Repair is proportionate to supplied harm
